svg.aria-label: Grafting: success depends on lining up the cambium (the thin green layer between bark and wood) of the scion and the rootstock and pressing them tightly together. Cleft grafting, around bud burst in spring, when the rootstock is fairly thick: leave 2-3 buds on the scion and make one cut on each side of its base to form a wedge about 3 cm long, slightly thicker on the outer side; saw the rootstock off about 5-10 cm above the ground and split the cut face down the middle about 3-4 cm deep; insert the scion so its outer cambium lines up with the cambium on one side of the rootstock, one scion on each side of a thick rootstock; tie firmly with plastic strip from the bottom up and seal the cut face and the scion tips with wax or clay. T-budding, late summer to early autumn: make a T-shaped cut in the rootstock about 5-10 cm above the ground; slice off a bud shield from about 1-1.5 cm below the bud to about 1 cm above it, cut off the leaf and keep the leaf stalk; slide the shield in from the top down, its top level with the cross-cut; tie firmly with plastic strip from the bottom up, leaving the bud and leaf stalk exposed; after about 10-15 days, if the leaf stalk drops off at a touch and the shield is fresh, the bud has taken; the next spring, before bud burst, cut the rootstock off about 1 cm above the bud
svg.title: Grafting: cleft grafting and T-budding

g.text: Key to success: line up the cambium of scion and rootstock
Scion: shoot or bud of the variety you want; rootstock: another rooted plant
Cambium: the thin green layer between the bark and the wood
Only close relatives take (e.g. apple on crab apple, pear on birch-leaf pear);
plants of different families basically never take
Sharp, clean knife; make each cut face in one smooth stroke; work fast:
do not touch the cut faces, get soil on them or let them dry out
